**Satish Chandra Kaushik** (13 April 1956 – 9 March 2023) was an Indian actor, director, producer, [comedian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedian "Comedian"), editor and [screenwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenwriter "Screenwriter"). He found fame in [Bollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi_cinema "Hindi cinema") with _[Mr. India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_India\_(1987\_film) "Mr. India (1987 film)")_ starring [Anil Kapoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anil_Kapoor "Anil Kapoor"), [Sridevi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sridevi "Sridevi"), and [Amrish Puri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrish_Puri "Amrish Puri"), where he played the iconic character of a cook named Calendar. He later directed films such as [Tere Naam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tere_Naam "Tere Naam").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Satish_Kaushik&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Kaushik was born in [Karol Bagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Bagh "Karol Bagh"), Delhi on 13 April 1956 into a Gaur Brahmin family.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-1) He graduated from [Kirori Mal College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirori_Mal_College "Kirori Mal College"), [Delhi University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_University "Delhi University") in 1972.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-2) He was an alumnus of [National School of Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_School_of_Drama "National School of Drama") and [Film and Television Institute of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_and_Television_Institute_of_India "Film and Television Institute of India").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-3)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Satish_Kaushik&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

As a film actor, he was noted for his roles as "Calendar" in _[Mr. India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_India\_(1987\_film) "Mr. India (1987 film)")_,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-4) as Pappu Pager in _[Deewana Mastana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deewana\_Mastana "Deewana Mastana")_, and as "Chanu Ahmed" in Sarah Gavron's British film _[Brick Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick\_Lane\_(2007\_film) "Brick Lane (2007 film)")_ (2007). He won the [Filmfare Best Comedian Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Best_Comedian_Award "Filmfare Best Comedian Award") twice: in 1990 for _[Ram Lakhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ram\_Lakhan "Ram Lakhan")_ and in 1997 for _[Saajan Chale Sasural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saajan\_Chale\_Sasural "Saajan Chale Sasural")._[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-5)

As a theatre actor, his most noted role was that of "[Willy Loman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy_Loman "Willy Loman")" in the Hindi-language play, _Salesman Ramlal,_ an adaptation of [Arthur Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Miller "Arthur Miller")'s _[Death of a Salesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death\_of\_a\_Salesman "Death of a Salesman")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-6) Kaushik wrote dialogues for [Kundan Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kundan_Shah "Kundan Shah")'s comedy classic _[Jaane Bhi Do Yaaron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaane\_Bhi\_Do\_Yaaro "Jaane Bhi Do Yaaro")_ (1983).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-7) His first film as a director was Anil Kapoor and Sridevi starrer _[Roop Ki Rani Choron Ka Raja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roop\_Ki\_Rani\_Choron\_Ka\_Raja\_(1993\_film) "Roop Ki Rani Choron Ka Raja (1993 film)")_ (1993). His second directorial was _Prem_ (1995), which was supposed to be [Tabu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabu_(actress) "Tabu (actress)")'s debut film. Both were box office disasters.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-8) He continued to make films and got his first hit with _[Hum Aapke Dil Mein Rehte Hain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hum\_Aapke\_Dil\_Mein\_Rehte\_Hain "Hum Aapke Dil Mein Rehte Hain")_ in 1999.

He co-wrote and anchored a TV countdown show, _Top Ten_, for which he won the Screen Videocon Award.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-9) In 2005, Kaushik directed [Arjun Rampal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjun_Rampal "Arjun Rampal"), [Amisha Patel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amisha_Patel "Amisha Patel"), and [Zayed Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_Khan "Zayed Khan") in _[Vaada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaada\_(2005\_film) "Vaada (2005 film)")_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-10) In 2007 Kaushik, together with [Anupam Kher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher "Anupam Kher"), who had been his classmate at [NSD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_School_of_Drama "National School of Drama"), launched a new film company called Karol Bagh Productions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-11) Their first film, _[Teree Sang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teree\_Sang "Teree Sang"),_ was directed by Satish Kaushik.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-12) Starring [Ruslaan Mumtaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruslaan_Mumtaz "Ruslaan Mumtaz") and [Sheena Shahabadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheena_Shahabadi "Sheena Shahabadi"), the film explores of teen pregnancy.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-13)

His next work was to be based on the life of [Tansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tansen "Tansen"), in which the role of Tansen was to be played by [Abhishek Bachchan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhishek_Bachchan "Abhishek Bachchan"), and the soundtrack was to be composed by [Ravindra Jain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravindra_Jain "Ravindra Jain"); the script for the film remains unfinished.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-14) Kaushik was working to promote [Haryana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haryana "Haryana")'s film industry, and was committed to making several films there.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-15)

### Chandigarh film city project

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Satish_Kaushik&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Chandigarh film city project")]

Kaushik was a partner in the [Chandigarh film city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandigarh_film_city "Chandigarh film city") project with real estate company Parsavnath Developers.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-16) They bought a 30-acre (12 ha) plot in Sarangpur Village, [Chandigarh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandigarh "Chandigarh") t a very attractive pricing.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-19)

## Personal life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Satish_Kaushik&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life and death")]

Kaushik married Shashi in 1985.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-20) Their son, Shanu, died in 1996 at age two.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-21) In 2012, their daughter was born through a [surrogate mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrogacy "Surrogacy").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-22)

Kaushik died of a heart attack in [Gurugram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurugram "Gurugram") on 9 March 2023, at the age of 66.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-24)

**Satish Chandra Kaushik** (13 April 1956 – 9 March 2023) was an Indian actor, director, producer, [comedian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedian "Comedian"), editor and [screenwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenwriter "Screenwriter"). He found fame in [Bollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi_cinema "Hindi cinema") with _[Mr. India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_India\_(1987\_film) "Mr. India (1987 film)")_ starring [Anil Kapoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anil_Kapoor "Anil Kapoor"), [Sridevi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sridevi "Sridevi"), and [Amrish Puri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrish_Puri "Amrish Puri"), where he played the iconic character of a cook named Calendar. He later directed films such as [Tere Naam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tere_Naam "Tere Naam").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Satish_Kaushik&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Kaushik was born in [Karol Bagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Bagh "Karol Bagh"), Delhi on 13 April 1956 into a Gaur Brahmin family.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-1) He graduated from [Kirori Mal College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirori_Mal_College "Kirori Mal College"), [Delhi University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_University "Delhi University") in 1972.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-2) He was an alumnus of [National School of Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_School_of_Drama "National School of Drama") and [Film and Television Institute of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_and_Television_Institute_of_India "Film and Television Institute of India").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-3)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Satish_Kaushik&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

As a film actor, he was noted for his roles as "Calendar" in _[Mr. India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_India\_(1987\_film) "Mr. India (1987 film)")_,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-4) as Pappu Pager in _[Deewana Mastana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deewana\_Mastana "Deewana Mastana")_, and as "Chanu Ahmed" in Sarah Gavron's British film _[Brick Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick\_Lane\_(2007\_film) "Brick Lane (2007 film)")_ (2007). He won the [Filmfare Best Comedian Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Best_Comedian_Award "Filmfare Best Comedian Award") twice: in 1990 for _[Ram Lakhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ram\_Lakhan "Ram Lakhan")_ and in 1997 for _[Saajan Chale Sasural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saajan\_Chale\_Sasural "Saajan Chale Sasural")._[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-5)

As a theatre actor, his most noted role was that of "[Willy Loman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy_Loman "Willy Loman")" in the Hindi-language play, _Salesman Ramlal,_ an adaptation of [Arthur Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Miller "Arthur Miller")'s _[Death of a Salesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death\_of\_a\_Salesman "Death of a Salesman")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-6) Kaushik wrote dialogues for [Kundan Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kundan_Shah "Kundan Shah")'s comedy classic _[Jaane Bhi Do Yaaron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaane\_Bhi\_Do\_Yaaro "Jaane Bhi Do Yaaro")_ (1983).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-7) His first film as a director was Anil Kapoor and Sridevi starrer _[Roop Ki Rani Choron Ka Raja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roop\_Ki\_Rani\_Choron\_Ka\_Raja\_(1993\_film) "Roop Ki Rani Choron Ka Raja (1993 film)")_ (1993). His second directorial was _Prem_ (1995), which was supposed to be [Tabu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabu_(actress) "Tabu (actress)")'s debut film. Both were box office disasters.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-8) He continued to make films and got his first hit with _[Hum Aapke Dil Mein Rehte Hain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hum\_Aapke\_Dil\_Mein\_Rehte\_Hain "Hum Aapke Dil Mein Rehte Hain")_ in 1999.

He co-wrote and anchored a TV countdown show, _Top Ten_, for which he won the Screen Videocon Award.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-9) In 2005, Kaushik directed [Arjun Rampal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjun_Rampal "Arjun Rampal"), [Amisha Patel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amisha_Patel "Amisha Patel"), and [Zayed Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_Khan "Zayed Khan") in _[Vaada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaada\_(2005\_film) "Vaada (2005 film)")_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-10) In 2007 Kaushik, together with [Anupam Kher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher "Anupam Kher"), who had been his classmate at [NSD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_School_of_Drama "National School of Drama"), launched a new film company called Karol Bagh Productions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-11) Their first film, _[Teree Sang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teree\_Sang "Teree Sang"),_ was directed by Satish Kaushik.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-12) Starring [Ruslaan Mumtaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruslaan_Mumtaz "Ruslaan Mumtaz") and [Sheena Shahabadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheena_Shahabadi "Sheena Shahabadi"), the film explores of teen pregnancy.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-13)

His next work was to be based on the life of [Tansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tansen "Tansen"), in which the role of Tansen was to be played by [Abhishek Bachchan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhishek_Bachchan "Abhishek Bachchan"), and the soundtrack was to be composed by [Ravindra Jain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravindra_Jain "Ravindra Jain"); the script for the film remains unfinished.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-14) Kaushik was working to promote [Haryana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haryana "Haryana")'s film industry, and was committed to making several films there.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-15)

### Chandigarh film city project

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Satish_Kaushik&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Chandigarh film city project")]

Kaushik was a partner in the [Chandigarh film city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandigarh_film_city "Chandigarh film city") project with real estate company Parsavnath Developers.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-16) They bought a 30-acre (12 ha) plot in Sarangpur Village, [Chandigarh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandigarh "Chandigarh") t a very attractive pricing.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-19)

## Personal life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Satish_Kaushik&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life and death")]

Kaushik married Shashi in 1985.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-20) Their son, Shanu, died in 1996 at age two.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-21) In 2012, their daughter was born through a [surrogate mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrogacy "Surrogacy").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-22)

Kaushik died of a heart attack in [Gurugram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurugram "Gurugram") on 9 March 2023, at the age of 66.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Kaushik#cite_note-24)

**Theatre of India** is one of the most ancient forms of theatre and it features a detailed textual, sculptural, and dramatic effects which emerged in mid [first millennium BC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_millennium_BC "1st millennium BC").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Lidova1994p1112-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-:0-2) Like in the areas of [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music") and [dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance "Dance"), the Indian theatre is also defined by the dramatic [performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performance_art "Performance art") based on the concept of _[Nritya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian\_classical\_dance "Indian classical dance")_, which is a [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") word for drama but encompasses dramatic narrative, virtuosic dance, and music.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-3)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-:0-2) Historically, Indian theatre has exerted influence beyond its borders, reaching ancient China and other countries in the Far East.

With the [Islamic conquests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_conquests_in_the_Indian_subcontinent "Muslim conquests in the Indian subcontinent") that began in the 10th and 11th centuries, theatre was discouraged or forbidden entirely.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Brandon_1997-4) Later, in an attempt to re-assert indigenous values and ideas, village theatre was encouraged across the subcontinent, developing in a large number of regional languages from the 15th to the 19th centuries.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-5) Modern Indian theatre developed during the [period of colonial rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") under the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"), from the mid-19th century until the mid-20th.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-6)

From the last half of the 19th century, theatres in India experienced a boost in numbers and practice. After [Indian independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India "Partition of India") in 1947, theatres spread throughout [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") as one of the means of entertainment. As a diverse, multi-cultural nation, the theatre of India cannot be reduced to a single, homogenous [trend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fad "Fad").

In contemporary India, the major competition with its theatre is that represented by growing [television industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television "Television") and the spread of films produced in the various [Indian film industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_India "Cinema of India"). Lack of finance is another major obstacle.

## History of Indian theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History of Indian theatre")]

### Sanskrit theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Sanskrit theatre")]

Main article: [Indian classical drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_classical_drama "Indian classical drama")

See also: [Koodiyattam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koodiyattam "Koodiyattam") and [Classical Indian musical theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Indian_musical_theatre "Classical Indian musical theatre")

The history of the origin of theatre in India is highly controversial.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

#### Early dating

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early dating")]

According to some scholars, Indian theatre emerged in the 15th century BC. Vedic text such as [Rigveda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigveda "Rigveda") provides evidence of drama plays being enacted during [Yagya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yagya "Yagya") ceremonies. The dialogues mentioned in the texts range from one person monologues to three person dialogues such as the dialogue between Indra, Indrani and Vrishakapi. The dialogues are not only religious in their context but also secular. For instance, one rigvedic monologue is about a gambler whose life is ruined because of it and has estranged his wife caves dating back to the 3rd century BC [[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-7) and [Khandagiri caves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udayagiri_and_Khandagiri_Caves "Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves") from the 2nd century BC are the earliest examples of theatre architecture in India.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-History_of_Indian_Theatre-8)

The dating of [Bhasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bh%C4%81sa "Bhāsa") is controversial and ranges from pre [Natyashastra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natya_Shastra "Natya Shastra") date of the 5th century BC [[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-History_of_Indian_Theatre-8) to the 2nd century AD. Bhasa according to some scholars preceded Natyashastra tradition. [Nandikeshvara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandikeshvara "Nandikeshvara") who wrote _Abhinaya Darpana_ lit. '_The Mirror of Gesture_' which itself was based on the abridgement of a long treatise of 400 sholakas called Bharatarnava,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-9) according to some scholars seems to have preceded Bharata. The most concrete example of Nandikeshvara's teachings have survived thanks to [Bhasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhasa "Bhasa").

Natyashastra, dated earliest to 200 BC, although mentions various teachers and call them acharya but doesn't name them, but it still ends with a reference to a lost treatise of dramatist Kohala.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-10)

#### Late dating

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Late dating")]

According to scholars who insist on late dating, Sanskrit theatre emerged in the 2nd century BCE and flourished between the 1st century CE and the 10th, which was a period of relative peace in the [history of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_India "History of India") during which hundreds of plays were written.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-11) Despite its name, Sanskrit theatre was not exclusively in [Sanskrit language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_language "Sanskrit language"). Other Indic languages collectively called as [Prakrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prakrit "Prakrit") were also used in addition to Sanskrit.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-RSZ21-12)

The earliest-surviving fragments of [Sanskrit drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_drama "Sanskrit drama") date from the 1st century CE.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-13) The wealth of archaeological evidence from earlier periods offers no indication of the existence of a tradition of theatre.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond516-14) The _[Vedas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedas "Vedas")_ (the earliest Indian literature, from between 1500 and 600 BCE) contain no hint of it; although a small number of hymns are composed in a form of [dialogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialogue "Dialogue"), the [rituals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritual "Ritual") of the [Vedic period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_period "Vedic period") do not appear to have developed into theatre.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond516-14) The _[Mahābhāṣya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mah%C4%81bh%C4%81%E1%B9%A3ya "Mahābhāṣya")_ by [Patañjali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pata%C3%B1jali "Patañjali") contains the earliest reference to what may have been the seeds of Sanskrit drama.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond517-15) This treatise on [grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammar "Grammar") from 140 BCE provides a feasible date for the beginnings of [theatre in India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_in_India "Theatre in India").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond517-15)

However, although there are no surviving fragments of any drama prior to this date, it is possible that early Buddhist literature provides the earliest evidence for the existence of Indian theater. The [Pali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pali "Pali")[suttas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutta_Pitaka "Sutta Pitaka") (ranging in date from the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE) refer to the existence of troupes of actors (led by a chief actor), who performed dramas on a stage. It is indicated that these dramas incorporated dance, but were listed as a distinct form of performance, alongside dancing, singing, and story recitations.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-16)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-18)

The major source of evidence for Sanskrit theatre is _[A Treatise on Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natyashastra "Natyashastra")_ (_Nātyaśāstra_), a compendium whose date of composition is uncertain (estimates range from 200 BCE to 200 CE) and whose authorship is attributed to [Bharata Muni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharata_Muni "Bharata Muni"). The _Treatise_ is the most complete work of dramaturgy in the ancient world. It addresses acting, dance, music, [dramatic construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramaturgy "Dramaturgy"), architecture, [costuming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costume_design "Costume design"), [make-up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatrical_makeup "Theatrical makeup"), [props](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatrical_properties "Theatrical properties"), the organisation of companies, the audience, competitions, and offers a [mythological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_mythology "Hindu mythology") account of the origin of theatre.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond517-15) In doing so, it provides indications about the nature of actual theatrical practices. Sanskrit theatre was performed on sacred ground by priests who had been trained in the necessary skills (dance, music, and recitation) in a [hereditary process]. Its aim was both to educate and to entertain. Characters in Sanskrit plays were important. They were broadly classified into three kinds which are Nayaka(hero), Nayika(heroine) and the Vidusaka(Clown).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-19)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%82%E0%B4%9F%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%AF%E0%B4%BE%E0%B4%9F%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9F%E0%B4%A4%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%A4%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%B2%E0%B5%86%E0%B4%B8%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%97%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%B0%E0%B5%80%E0%B4%B5%E0%B5%BB.jpg/250px-%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%82%E0%B4%9F%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%AF%E0%B4%BE%E0%B4%9F%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9F%E0%B4%A4%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%A4%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%B2%E0%B5%86%E0%B4%B8%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%97%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%B0%E0%B5%80%E0%B4%B5%E0%B5%BB.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%82%E0%B4%9F%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%AF%E0%B4%BE%E0%B4%9F%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9F%E0%B4%A4%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%A4%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%B2%E0%B5%86%E0%B4%B8%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%97%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%B0%E0%B5%80%E0%B4%B5%E0%B5%BB.jpg)

Performer playing [Sugriva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugriva "Sugriva") in the [Koodiyattam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koodiyattam "Koodiyattam") form of [Sanskrit theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_drama "Sanskrit drama")

An appreciation for the stagecraft and classic Sanskrit drama was seen as an essential part of a sophisticated world view, by the end of the seventh century.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-20) Under the patronage of royal courts, performers belonged to professional companies that were directed by a stage manager (_sutradhar_), who may also have acted.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-21) This task was thought of as being analogous to that of a [puppeteer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppetry "Puppetry")—the literal meaning of "_sutradhar_" is "holder of the strings or threads".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond517-15) The performers were trained rigorously in vocal and physical technique.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-22) There were no prohibitions against female performers; companies were all-male, all-female, and of mixed gender. Certain sentiments were considered inappropriate for men to enact, however, and were thought better suited to women. Some performers played characters their own age, while others played ages different from their own (whether younger or older). Of all the elements of theatre, the _Treatise_ gives most attention to acting (_abhinaya_), which consists of two styles: realistic (_lokadharmi_) and conventional (_natyadharmi_), though the major focus is on the latter.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-23)

Its drama is regarded as the highest achievement of [Sanskrit literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_literature "Sanskrit literature").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Brandonxvii-24) It used [stock characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_character "Stock character"), such as the hero (_nayaka_), heroine (_nayika_), or clown (_vidusaka_). Actors may have specialised in a particular type. [Kālidāsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81lid%C4%81sa "Kālidāsa") is arguably considered to be [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India")'s greatest Sanskrit dramatist, writing in the ca. 4th century CE-ca. 5th century CE. Three famous romantic plays written by Kālidāsa are the _[Mālavikāgnimitram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81lavik%C4%81gnimitram "Mālavikāgnimitram")_ (_Mālavikā and Agnimitra_), _[Vikramuurvashiiya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vikramuurvashiiya "Vikramuurvashiiya")_ (_Pertaining to Vikrama and Urvashi_), and _[Abhijñānaśākuntala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Recognition\_of\_Sakuntala "The Recognition of Sakuntala")_ (_The Recognition of Shakuntala_). The last was inspired by a story in the _Mahabharata_ and is the most famous. It was the first to be translated into English and German. _[Śakuntalā](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhij%C3%B1%C4%81na%C5%9B%C4%81kuntalam "Abhijñānaśākuntalam")_ (in English translation) influenced [Goethe's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Wolfgang_von_Goethe "Johann Wolfgang von Goethe")_[Faust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goethe's\_Faust "Goethe's Faust")_ (1808–1832).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Brandonxvii-24)

The next great Indian dramatist was [Bhavabhuti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhavabhuti "Bhavabhuti") (c. 7th century CE). He is said to have written the following three plays: _Malati-Madhava_, _Mahaviracharita_ and _Uttar Ramacharita_. Among these three, the last two cover between them the entire epic of _Ramayana_. The powerful Indian emperor [Harsha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harsha "Harsha") (606–648) is credited with having written three plays: the comedy _[Ratnavali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratnavali "Ratnavali")_, _[Priyadarsika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priyadarsika "Priyadarsika")_, and the [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist "Buddhist") drama _[Nagananda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagananda "Nagananda")_.

According to some scholars the earliest form of the classical theatre of India was the [Sanskrit theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_drama "Sanskrit drama") which came into existence after the development of [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_theatre "Greek theatre") and [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_theatre_(structure) "Roman theatre (structure)") theatre.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-RSZ12-25) One theory describes this development as an offshoot of Alexander the Great's Indian conquest.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-:1-26) The invading army staged Greek-style plays and Indians picked up the performance art. While some scholars argue that traditional Indian theatre predated it, there is a recognition that classical Greek theatre has helped transformed it.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-:1-26) The Greek origin of Indian theatre has not received popular acceptance.

### Theatre in medieval India

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Theatre in medieval India")]

India's artistic identity is deeply routed within its social, economical, cultural, and religious views. For this reason it is essential to understand Indian cultural practices as they relate directly to performers and performances of this time. Performances including dance, music, and text are an expression of devotion for the Indian culture, so when looking at 'theatre' of this time a broader definition must be ascribed to the word.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Trivedi_73%E2%80%93110-27)

Based on the understanding that performing arts are audience-oriented and must continuously adapt to the socio-cultural landscape of their patronage. Northern India managed to retain their cultural traditions in spite of the new Turko-Persian influences. The early thirteenth century marked this change for the Indian culture, where Sanskrit dramas and stage craft had been previously revered by the elites, it was now no longer relevant. This was due to the invading cultures that began to dominate and did not appreciate or understand, and since they did not understand the Sanskrit language it could no longer be held in such a high regard, and as a consequence many theatre artist suffered from neglect.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Trivedi_73%E2%80%93110-27)

The commonplace to find performers was in urban centers, because it was there they were able to find work to support themselves. Large temples where home to musical and theatrical shows.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Trivedi_73%E2%80%93110-27)

A Bharata Natyshatra also known as the śāstra was written to list costumes, gestures, positions of the body, and make up. It also lists plots that were weighed unsuitable and it also the most completed document. Most of Indian theatre had no scenery. There was usually a few props like a brass lamp.

When the concept of "Theatrical Art" was introduced, medieval India was narrating poems. [Bhakti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhakti "Bhakti") poetry became popular.

During medieval India [Bhavabhuti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhavabhuti "Bhavabhuti") was a famous dramatist, he had three portent plays Malati-Madhava, Magviracharita and the Uttar Ramacharita.

### Theatre in India under the British

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Theatre in India under the British")]

Under British colonial rule, modern Indian theatre began when a theatre was started in [Belgachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgachia "Belgachia"). One of the earliest plays composed and staged during this period was Buro Shalikher Ghaare Roa (1860) by [Michael Madhusudan Dutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Madhusudan_Dutt "Michael Madhusudan Dutt"), both in [Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"). Around the same time, [Nil Darpan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nil_Darpan "Nil Darpan") (1858–59, first commercial production in 1872, by [Girish Chandra Ghosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Chandra_Ghosh "Girish Chandra Ghosh") at the national theatre in [Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcutta "Calcutta")) a Bengali play by [Dinabandhu Mitra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinabandhu_Mitra "Dinabandhu Mitra") garnered both accolades and controversy for depicting the horror and tragedy of indigo cultivation in rural Bengal, and played a major role in the [indigo revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigo_revolt "Indigo revolt"). Rabindranath Tagore was a pioneering modern playwright who wrote plays noted for their exploration and questioning of nationalism, identity, spiritualism and material greed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Banham1051-28) His plays are written in [Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language") and include _Chitra_ (_Chitrangada_, 1892), _The King of the Dark Chamber_ (_Raja_, 1910), _[The Post Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Post\_Office\_(play) "The Post Office (play)")_ (_Dakghar_, 1913), and _Red Oleander_ (_Raktakarabi_, 1924).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Banham1051-28)

[Kalyanam Raghuramaiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyanam_Raghuramaiah "Kalyanam Raghuramaiah"), a recipient of the [Sangeet Natak Akademi Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangeet_Natak_Akademi_Award "Sangeet Natak Akademi Award"), and the [Padmashri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padmashri "Padmashri"), was known for the roles of [Krishna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krishna "Krishna") or Dushyantha, Bhavanisankar, Narada etc. in [Telugu theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telugu_theatre "Telugu theatre"). He performed those roles for about 60 years. He indulged in elaborate raga alapana, based on different [ragas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raga "Raga") while rendering padyams.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-blogspot1-30) One of the finest method actors, He had the ability to sing padyams and songs through whistle, by putting his finger in mouth and producing the [whistle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whistle "Whistle") or flute sound (meaning Eela in Telugu). He has acted in various dramas and gave more than 20,000 stage performances.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Brandon_1997-4) He was called the "Nightingale of the Stage" by [Rabindranath Tagore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore "Rabindranath Tagore").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-eenadu1-31)

The British believed that the Indian actors were mystical creatures. They believed they brought them luck and prosperity. The emergent modern Indian theater, which is also referred to as Native theatre, features a theatrical approach that has been viewed as an intersection of Indian social space with Western theater formats and [conventions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramatic_convention "Dramatic convention").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-32) The resulting theatrical space is described to be existing at the material, symbolic, and discursive levels. To resist its use by Indians as an instrument of protest against colonial rule, the British Government imposed the [Dramatic Performances Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramatic_Performances_Act "Dramatic Performances Act") in 1876.

### Indian theatre after Independence (1947–1992)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Indian theatre after Independence (1947–1992)")]

The Modern Endangered Archives Program funded a digitization project carried out by Natarang Pratishthan which digitized theatre brochures from 1946 to present. These brochures provide information on what plays were performed during this period as well as provide an anthropological source of who/what sustained theatre in both big and small cities around India.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-33) This collection of brochures is available through the UCLA library.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-34)

#### Improvisation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Improvisation")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Vikhyath_Mysore.jpg/250px-Vikhyath_Mysore.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vikhyath_Mysore.jpg)

Actor playing the role of Mohammad Bin Tughlak

[Improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisational "Improvisational") (also known as improv or impro) is a form of theatre in which the actors use [improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation") acting techniques to perform spontaneously. Improvisers typically use audience suggestions to guide the performance as they create dialogue, setting, and plot extemporaneously.

Many improvisational actors also work as scripted actors and "improv" techniques are often taught in standard acting classes. The basic skills of listening, clarity, confidence, and performing instinctively and spontaneously are considered important skills for actors to develop.

Improvisational theatre in India is largely used for educational, interventional and entertainment purposes. The traces of improvisational theatre in India date back to the 1990s with the advent of [Forum theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forum_theatre "Forum theatre") with [Jana Sanskriti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_the_Oppressed#Jana_Sanskriti "Theatre of the Oppressed") under the leadership of [Sanjoy Ganguly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_the_Oppressed#Dr_Sanjoy_Ganguly "Theatre of the Oppressed"). After that in 1999, a team from the US with Bev Hoskins and Mary Good introduced [Playback theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playback_theatre "Playback theatre") to India. Thus Playback theatre and Forum theatre began to take shape in the remotest parts of India, such as Karur, Chennai, West Bengal, as well as Bangalore. [Yours Truly Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yours_Truly_Theatre,_Bangalore "Yours Truly Theatre, Bangalore"), a Bangalore-based group, developed "complete the story", an indigenous format of improvisational theatre developed under the leadership of Ranji David and Nandini Rao in 2006. In 2009, they also developed another form of improvisational theatre called "mushyara theatre".

In the late 1960s Badal Sircar introduced a new form of political theatre called the Third Theatre. Badal Sarkar's anti-establishment experimental theatre created a new genre of social enlightenment. He formed his first Third Theatre Group satabdi, in the year 1967. They used to perform Drama written by Badal Sircar in Anganmancha (theatre in the courtyard) in the Third Theatre form that break away from the tradition of One point view of the Proscenium and urged on the taking theatre to the people.

## Forms of Indian theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Forms of Indian theatre")]

### Traditional Indian theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Traditional Indian theatre")]

Main article: [List of traditional Indian theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_traditional_Indian_theatre "List of traditional Indian theatre")

[Kutiyattam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutiyattam "Kutiyattam") is the only surviving specimen of the ancient Sanskrit theatre, thought to have originated around the beginning of the [Common Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era"), and is officially recognised by [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") as a [Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masterpiece_of_the_Oral_and_Intangible_Heritage_of_Humanity "Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity"). In addition, many forms of Indian folk theatre abound. [Bhavai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhavai "Bhavai") (strolling players) is a popular folk theatre form of [Gujarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujarat "Gujarat"), said to have arisen in the 14th century AD. [Bhaona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhaona "Bhaona") and [Ankiya Nats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankiya_Nat "Ankiya Nat") have been practicing in [Assam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assam "Assam") since the early 16th century which were created and initiated by [Mahapurusha Srimanta Sankardeva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahapurusha_Srimanta_Sankardeva "Mahapurusha Srimanta Sankardeva"). [Jatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jatra_(Bengal) "Jatra (Bengal)") has been popular in [Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal "Bengal") and its origin is traced to the Bhakti movement in the 16th century. Another folk theatre form popular in [Haryana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haryana "Haryana"), Uttar Pradesh and [Malwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malwa "Malwa") region of [Madhya Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madhya_Pradesh "Madhya Pradesh") is [Swang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swang_(dance_drama) "Swang (dance drama)"), which is dialogue-oriented rather than movement-oriented and is considered to have arisen in its present form in the late 18th – early 19th centuries.

[Yakshagana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakshagana "Yakshagana") is a very popular theatre art in Karnataka and has existed under different names at least since the 16th century. It is semi-classical in nature and involves music and songs based on [carnatic music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnatic_music "Carnatic music"), rich costumes, storylines based on the _[Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata")_ and _[Ramayana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramayana "Ramayana")._ It also employs spoken dialogue in-between its songs that gives it a [folk art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_art "Folk art") flavour. [Kathakali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathakali "Kathakali") is a form of dance-drama, characteristic of [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"), that arose in the 17th century, developing from the temple-art plays [Krishnanattam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krishnanattam "Krishnanattam") and [Ramanattam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanattam "Ramanattam").

### Urdu/Hindustani theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Urdu/Hindustani theatre")]

Urdu drama evolved from the prevailing dramatic traditions of North India shaping Rahas or Raas as practiced by exponents like [Wajid Ali Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wajid_Ali_Shah "Wajid Ali Shah"), [Nawab of Awadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawab_of_Awadh "Nawab of Awadh"). His dramatic experiments led to the famous _[Inder Sabha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inder\_Sabha "Inder Sabha")_ of [Agha Hasan Amanat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agha_Hasan_Amanat "Agha Hasan Amanat"), and later this tradition took the shape of [Parsi theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsi_theatre "Parsi theatre"). _[Yahudi Ki Ladki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahudi\_Ki\_Ladki "Yahudi Ki Ladki")_ (_The Jew's Daughter_) by [Agha Hashar Kashmiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agha_Hashar_Kashmiri "Agha Hashar Kashmiri") is the culmination of this tradition.

Among all the languages Urdu (which was called Hindi by early writers), along with Gujrati, Marathi and Bengali theatres have kept flourishing and demand for its writers and artists has not subsided by the drama aficionados. All the early gems of Urdu theatre (performed by Parsi Companies) were made into films. Great works like those by Shakespeare have influenced modern Urdu tradition to a large extent when Indian, Iranian, Turkish stories and folk was adapted for stage with heavy doses of Urdu poetry. In modern times writers like [Imtiaz Ali Taj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imtiaz_Ali_Taj "Imtiaz Ali Taj"), Rafi Peer, Krishan Chander, Manto, Upender Nath Ashk, Ghulam Rabbani, Prof. Mujeeb and many others shaped this tradition.

While Prof Hasan, Ghulam Jeelani, J.N. Kaushal, Shameem Hanfi, Jameel Shaidayi etc. belong to the old generation, contemporary writers like Mujeeb Khan, [Javed Siddiqui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javed_Siddiqui "Javed Siddiqui"), Sayeed Alam, Danish Iqbal, Anis Azmi, Aftab Hasnain, Aslam Parvez, Anis Javed, Iqbal Niyazi, [Syed Sahil Agha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syed_Sahil_Agha "Syed Sahil Agha") and Zaheer Anwar are postmodern playwrights actively contributing in the field of Urdu drama.

Zaheer Anwar has kept the flag of Urdu theatre flying in Kolkata. Unlike the writers of previous generations, Danish iqbal and Zaheer do not write bookish plays but their work is a product of a vigorous performing tradition. Iqbal Niyazi of Mumbai has written several plays in Urdu. His play _Aur Kitne Jalyanwala BaughU??_ won a national award and other awards. Hence this is the only generation after Amanat and Agha Hashr who actually write for the stage and not for libraries.

The group Aatrangi Pitaara Foundation is actively performing and saving Hindustani theatre. Their presentation of _Anti-National Ghalib_,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-35) written by Danish Iqbal, has been well received by the Delhi Theatre enthusiasts. Leading the group, [Keshav Raina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keshav_Raina?action=edit&redlink=1 "Keshav Raina (page does not exist)") is developing more Hindustani shows showcasing the rich history and heritage of India.

### Indian puppet theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Indian puppet theatre")]

[Yakshagana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakshagana "Yakshagana") is a popular semi-classical theatre art from coastal Karnataka. It uses rich costumes, music, dance, and dialogue. Puppet shows in parts of Karnataka uses all these elements of [yakshagana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakshagana "Yakshagana") to depict stories from the _[Ramayana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramayana "Ramayana")_ and _[Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata")._

### Mobile theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Mobile theatre")]

Mobile theatres are a kind of popular theatre form that exist mainly in [Assam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assam "Assam").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] For staging their plays, theatre groups travel different places with their casts, singers, musicians, dancers and entire crew. Even the tent and chairs for the audience are carried with them. Mobile theatre was first staged on 2 October 1963 in [Pathsala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathsala "Pathsala"), Assam. [Achyut Lahkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achyut_Lahkar "Achyut Lahkar") is known as the father of mobile theatre.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-36)

**Theatre of India** is one of the most ancient forms of theatre and it features a detailed textual, sculptural, and dramatic effects which emerged in mid [first millennium BC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_millennium_BC "1st millennium BC").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Lidova1994p1112-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-:0-2) Like in the areas of [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music") and [dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance "Dance"), the Indian theatre is also defined by the dramatic [performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performance_art "Performance art") based on the concept of _[Nritya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian\_classical\_dance "Indian classical dance")_, which is a [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") word for drama but encompasses dramatic narrative, virtuosic dance, and music.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-3)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-:0-2) Historically, Indian theatre has exerted influence beyond its borders, reaching ancient China and other countries in the Far East.

With the [Islamic conquests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_conquests_in_the_Indian_subcontinent "Muslim conquests in the Indian subcontinent") that began in the 10th and 11th centuries, theatre was discouraged or forbidden entirely.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Brandon_1997-4) Later, in an attempt to re-assert indigenous values and ideas, village theatre was encouraged across the subcontinent, developing in a large number of regional languages from the 15th to the 19th centuries.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-5) Modern Indian theatre developed during the [period of colonial rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") under the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"), from the mid-19th century until the mid-20th.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-6)

From the last half of the 19th century, theatres in India experienced a boost in numbers and practice. After [Indian independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India "Partition of India") in 1947, theatres spread throughout [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") as one of the means of entertainment. As a diverse, multi-cultural nation, the theatre of India cannot be reduced to a single, homogenous [trend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fad "Fad").

In contemporary India, the major competition with its theatre is that represented by growing [television industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television "Television") and the spread of films produced in the various [Indian film industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_India "Cinema of India"). Lack of finance is another major obstacle.

## History of Indian theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History of Indian theatre")]

### Sanskrit theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Sanskrit theatre")]

Main article: [Indian classical drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_classical_drama "Indian classical drama")

See also: [Koodiyattam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koodiyattam "Koodiyattam") and [Classical Indian musical theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Indian_musical_theatre "Classical Indian musical theatre")

The history of the origin of theatre in India is highly controversial.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

#### Early dating

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early dating")]

According to some scholars, Indian theatre emerged in the 15th century BC. Vedic text such as [Rigveda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigveda "Rigveda") provides evidence of drama plays being enacted during [Yagya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yagya "Yagya") ceremonies. The dialogues mentioned in the texts range from one person monologues to three person dialogues such as the dialogue between Indra, Indrani and Vrishakapi. The dialogues are not only religious in their context but also secular. For instance, one rigvedic monologue is about a gambler whose life is ruined because of it and has estranged his wife caves dating back to the 3rd century BC [[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-7) and [Khandagiri caves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udayagiri_and_Khandagiri_Caves "Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves") from the 2nd century BC are the earliest examples of theatre architecture in India.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-History_of_Indian_Theatre-8)

The dating of [Bhasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bh%C4%81sa "Bhāsa") is controversial and ranges from pre [Natyashastra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natya_Shastra "Natya Shastra") date of the 5th century BC [[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-History_of_Indian_Theatre-8) to the 2nd century AD. Bhasa according to some scholars preceded Natyashastra tradition. [Nandikeshvara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandikeshvara "Nandikeshvara") who wrote _Abhinaya Darpana_ lit. '_The Mirror of Gesture_' which itself was based on the abridgement of a long treatise of 400 sholakas called Bharatarnava,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-9) according to some scholars seems to have preceded Bharata. The most concrete example of Nandikeshvara's teachings have survived thanks to [Bhasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhasa "Bhasa").

Natyashastra, dated earliest to 200 BC, although mentions various teachers and call them acharya but doesn't name them, but it still ends with a reference to a lost treatise of dramatist Kohala.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-10)

#### Late dating

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Late dating")]

According to scholars who insist on late dating, Sanskrit theatre emerged in the 2nd century BCE and flourished between the 1st century CE and the 10th, which was a period of relative peace in the [history of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_India "History of India") during which hundreds of plays were written.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-11) Despite its name, Sanskrit theatre was not exclusively in [Sanskrit language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_language "Sanskrit language"). Other Indic languages collectively called as [Prakrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prakrit "Prakrit") were also used in addition to Sanskrit.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-RSZ21-12)

The earliest-surviving fragments of [Sanskrit drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_drama "Sanskrit drama") date from the 1st century CE.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-13) The wealth of archaeological evidence from earlier periods offers no indication of the existence of a tradition of theatre.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond516-14) The _[Vedas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedas "Vedas")_ (the earliest Indian literature, from between 1500 and 600 BCE) contain no hint of it; although a small number of hymns are composed in a form of [dialogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialogue "Dialogue"), the [rituals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritual "Ritual") of the [Vedic period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_period "Vedic period") do not appear to have developed into theatre.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond516-14) The _[Mahābhāṣya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mah%C4%81bh%C4%81%E1%B9%A3ya "Mahābhāṣya")_ by [Patañjali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pata%C3%B1jali "Patañjali") contains the earliest reference to what may have been the seeds of Sanskrit drama.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond517-15) This treatise on [grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammar "Grammar") from 140 BCE provides a feasible date for the beginnings of [theatre in India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_in_India "Theatre in India").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond517-15)

However, although there are no surviving fragments of any drama prior to this date, it is possible that early Buddhist literature provides the earliest evidence for the existence of Indian theater. The [Pali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pali "Pali")[suttas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutta_Pitaka "Sutta Pitaka") (ranging in date from the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE) refer to the existence of troupes of actors (led by a chief actor), who performed dramas on a stage. It is indicated that these dramas incorporated dance, but were listed as a distinct form of performance, alongside dancing, singing, and story recitations.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-16)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-18)

The major source of evidence for Sanskrit theatre is _[A Treatise on Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natyashastra "Natyashastra")_ (_Nātyaśāstra_), a compendium whose date of composition is uncertain (estimates range from 200 BCE to 200 CE) and whose authorship is attributed to [Bharata Muni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharata_Muni "Bharata Muni"). The _Treatise_ is the most complete work of dramaturgy in the ancient world. It addresses acting, dance, music, [dramatic construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramaturgy "Dramaturgy"), architecture, [costuming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costume_design "Costume design"), [make-up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatrical_makeup "Theatrical makeup"), [props](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatrical_properties "Theatrical properties"), the organisation of companies, the audience, competitions, and offers a [mythological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_mythology "Hindu mythology") account of the origin of theatre.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond517-15) In doing so, it provides indications about the nature of actual theatrical practices. Sanskrit theatre was performed on sacred ground by priests who had been trained in the necessary skills (dance, music, and recitation) in a [hereditary process]. Its aim was both to educate and to entertain. Characters in Sanskrit plays were important. They were broadly classified into three kinds which are Nayaka(hero), Nayika(heroine) and the Vidusaka(Clown).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-19)

Performer playing [Sugriva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugriva "Sugriva") in the [Koodiyattam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koodiyattam "Koodiyattam") form of [Sanskrit theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_drama "Sanskrit drama")

An appreciation for the stagecraft and classic Sanskrit drama was seen as an essential part of a sophisticated world view, by the end of the seventh century.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-20) Under the patronage of royal courts, performers belonged to professional companies that were directed by a stage manager (_sutradhar_), who may also have acted.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-21) This task was thought of as being analogous to that of a [puppeteer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppetry "Puppetry")—the literal meaning of "_sutradhar_" is "holder of the strings or threads".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Richmond517-15) The performers were trained rigorously in vocal and physical technique.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-22) There were no prohibitions against female performers; companies were all-male, all-female, and of mixed gender. Certain sentiments were considered inappropriate for men to enact, however, and were thought better suited to women. Some performers played characters their own age, while others played ages different from their own (whether younger or older). Of all the elements of theatre, the _Treatise_ gives most attention to acting (_abhinaya_), which consists of two styles: realistic (_lokadharmi_) and conventional (_natyadharmi_), though the major focus is on the latter.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-23)

Its drama is regarded as the highest achievement of [Sanskrit literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_literature "Sanskrit literature").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Brandonxvii-24) It used [stock characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_character "Stock character"), such as the hero (_nayaka_), heroine (_nayika_), or clown (_vidusaka_). Actors may have specialised in a particular type. [Kālidāsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81lid%C4%81sa "Kālidāsa") is arguably considered to be [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India")'s greatest Sanskrit dramatist, writing in the ca. 4th century CE-ca. 5th century CE. Three famous romantic plays written by Kālidāsa are the _[Mālavikāgnimitram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81lavik%C4%81gnimitram "Mālavikāgnimitram")_ (_Mālavikā and Agnimitra_), _[Vikramuurvashiiya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vikramuurvashiiya "Vikramuurvashiiya")_ (_Pertaining to Vikrama and Urvashi_), and _[Abhijñānaśākuntala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Recognition\_of\_Sakuntala "The Recognition of Sakuntala")_ (_The Recognition of Shakuntala_). The last was inspired by a story in the _Mahabharata_ and is the most famous. It was the first to be translated into English and German. _[Śakuntalā](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhij%C3%B1%C4%81na%C5%9B%C4%81kuntalam "Abhijñānaśākuntalam")_ (in English translation) influenced [Goethe's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Wolfgang_von_Goethe "Johann Wolfgang von Goethe")_[Faust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goethe's\_Faust "Goethe's Faust")_ (1808–1832).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Brandonxvii-24)

The next great Indian dramatist was [Bhavabhuti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhavabhuti "Bhavabhuti") (c. 7th century CE). He is said to have written the following three plays: _Malati-Madhava_, _Mahaviracharita_ and _Uttar Ramacharita_. Among these three, the last two cover between them the entire epic of _Ramayana_. The powerful Indian emperor [Harsha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harsha "Harsha") (606–648) is credited with having written three plays: the comedy _[Ratnavali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratnavali "Ratnavali")_, _[Priyadarsika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priyadarsika "Priyadarsika")_, and the [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist "Buddhist") drama _[Nagananda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagananda "Nagananda")_.

According to some scholars the earliest form of the classical theatre of India was the [Sanskrit theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_drama "Sanskrit drama") which came into existence after the development of [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_theatre "Greek theatre") and [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_theatre_(structure) "Roman theatre (structure)") theatre.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-RSZ12-25) One theory describes this development as an offshoot of Alexander the Great's Indian conquest.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-:1-26) The invading army staged Greek-style plays and Indians picked up the performance art. While some scholars argue that traditional Indian theatre predated it, there is a recognition that classical Greek theatre has helped transformed it.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-:1-26) The Greek origin of Indian theatre has not received popular acceptance.

### Theatre in medieval India

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Theatre in medieval India")]

India's artistic identity is deeply routed within its social, economical, cultural, and religious views. For this reason it is essential to understand Indian cultural practices as they relate directly to performers and performances of this time. Performances including dance, music, and text are an expression of devotion for the Indian culture, so when looking at 'theatre' of this time a broader definition must be ascribed to the word.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Trivedi_73%E2%80%93110-27)

Based on the understanding that performing arts are audience-oriented and must continuously adapt to the socio-cultural landscape of their patronage. Northern India managed to retain their cultural traditions in spite of the new Turko-Persian influences. The early thirteenth century marked this change for the Indian culture, where Sanskrit dramas and stage craft had been previously revered by the elites, it was now no longer relevant. This was due to the invading cultures that began to dominate and did not appreciate or understand, and since they did not understand the Sanskrit language it could no longer be held in such a high regard, and as a consequence many theatre artist suffered from neglect.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Trivedi_73%E2%80%93110-27)

The commonplace to find performers was in urban centers, because it was there they were able to find work to support themselves. Large temples where home to musical and theatrical shows.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Trivedi_73%E2%80%93110-27)

A Bharata Natyshatra also known as the śāstra was written to list costumes, gestures, positions of the body, and make up. It also lists plots that were weighed unsuitable and it also the most completed document. Most of Indian theatre had no scenery. There was usually a few props like a brass lamp.

When the concept of "Theatrical Art" was introduced, medieval India was narrating poems. [Bhakti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhakti "Bhakti") poetry became popular.

During medieval India [Bhavabhuti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhavabhuti "Bhavabhuti") was a famous dramatist, he had three portent plays Malati-Madhava, Magviracharita and the Uttar Ramacharita.

### Theatre in India under the British

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Theatre in India under the British")]

Under British colonial rule, modern Indian theatre began when a theatre was started in [Belgachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgachia "Belgachia"). One of the earliest plays composed and staged during this period was Buro Shalikher Ghaare Roa (1860) by [Michael Madhusudan Dutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Madhusudan_Dutt "Michael Madhusudan Dutt"), both in [Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"). Around the same time, [Nil Darpan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nil_Darpan "Nil Darpan") (1858–59, first commercial production in 1872, by [Girish Chandra Ghosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Chandra_Ghosh "Girish Chandra Ghosh") at the national theatre in [Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcutta "Calcutta")) a Bengali play by [Dinabandhu Mitra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinabandhu_Mitra "Dinabandhu Mitra") garnered both accolades and controversy for depicting the horror and tragedy of indigo cultivation in rural Bengal, and played a major role in the [indigo revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigo_revolt "Indigo revolt"). Rabindranath Tagore was a pioneering modern playwright who wrote plays noted for their exploration and questioning of nationalism, identity, spiritualism and material greed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Banham1051-28) His plays are written in [Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language") and include _Chitra_ (_Chitrangada_, 1892), _The King of the Dark Chamber_ (_Raja_, 1910), _[The Post Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Post\_Office\_(play) "The Post Office (play)")_ (_Dakghar_, 1913), and _Red Oleander_ (_Raktakarabi_, 1924).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Banham1051-28)

[Kalyanam Raghuramaiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyanam_Raghuramaiah "Kalyanam Raghuramaiah"), a recipient of the [Sangeet Natak Akademi Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangeet_Natak_Akademi_Award "Sangeet Natak Akademi Award"), and the [Padmashri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padmashri "Padmashri"), was known for the roles of [Krishna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krishna "Krishna") or Dushyantha, Bhavanisankar, Narada etc. in [Telugu theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telugu_theatre "Telugu theatre"). He performed those roles for about 60 years. He indulged in elaborate raga alapana, based on different [ragas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raga "Raga") while rendering padyams.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-blogspot1-30) One of the finest method actors, He had the ability to sing padyams and songs through whistle, by putting his finger in mouth and producing the [whistle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whistle "Whistle") or flute sound (meaning Eela in Telugu). He has acted in various dramas and gave more than 20,000 stage performances.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-Brandon_1997-4) He was called the "Nightingale of the Stage" by [Rabindranath Tagore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore "Rabindranath Tagore").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-eenadu1-31)

The British believed that the Indian actors were mystical creatures. They believed they brought them luck and prosperity. The emergent modern Indian theater, which is also referred to as Native theatre, features a theatrical approach that has been viewed as an intersection of Indian social space with Western theater formats and [conventions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramatic_convention "Dramatic convention").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-32) The resulting theatrical space is described to be existing at the material, symbolic, and discursive levels. To resist its use by Indians as an instrument of protest against colonial rule, the British Government imposed the [Dramatic Performances Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramatic_Performances_Act "Dramatic Performances Act") in 1876.

### Indian theatre after Independence (1947–1992)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Indian theatre after Independence (1947–1992)")]

The Modern Endangered Archives Program funded a digitization project carried out by Natarang Pratishthan which digitized theatre brochures from 1946 to present. These brochures provide information on what plays were performed during this period as well as provide an anthropological source of who/what sustained theatre in both big and small cities around India.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-33) This collection of brochures is available through the UCLA library.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_theatre#cite_note-34)

#### Improvisation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_of_India&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Improvisation")]

Actor playing the role of Mohammad Bin Tughlak

[Improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisational "Improvisational") (also known as improv or impro) is a form of theatre in which the actors use [improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation") acting techniques to perform spontaneously. Improvisers typically use audience suggestions to guide the performance as they create dialogue, setting, and plot extemporaneously.

Many improvisational actors also work as scripted actors and "improv" techniques are often taught in standard acting classes. The basic skills of listening, clarity, confidence, and performing instinctively and spontaneously are considered important skills for actors to develop.

Improvisational theatre in India is largely used for educational, interventional and entertainment purposes. The traces of improvisational theatre in India date back to the 1990s with the advent of [Forum theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forum_theatre "Forum theatre") with [Jana Sanskriti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_the_Oppressed#Jana_Sanskriti "Theatre of the Oppressed") under the leadership of [Sanjoy Ganguly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_the_Oppressed#Dr_Sanjoy_Ganguly "Theatre of the Oppressed"). After that in 1999, a team from the US with Bev Hoskins and Mary Good introduced [Playback theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playback_theatre "Playback theatre") to India. Thus Playback theatre and Forum theatre began to take shape in the remotest parts of India, such as Karur, Chennai, West Bengal, as well as Bangalore. [Yours Truly Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yours_Truly_Theatre,_Bangalore "Yours Truly Theatre, Bangalore"), a Bangalore-based group, developed "complete the story", an indigenous format of improvisational theatre developed under the leadership of Ranji David and Nandini Rao in 2006. In 2009, they also developed another form of improvisational theatre called "mushyara theatre".

In the late 1960s Badal Sircar introduced a new form of political theatre called the Third Theatre. Badal Sarkar's anti-establishment experimental theatre created a new genre of social enlightenment. He formed his first Third Theatre Group satabdi, in the year 1967. They used to perform Drama written by Badal Sircar in Anganmancha (theatre in the courtyard) in the Third Theatre form that break away from the tradition of One point view of the Proscenium and urged on the taking theatre to the people.
