His other box office hits of this period, include _[Beta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta\_(film) "Beta (film)")_ (1992), _[Shola Aur Shabnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shola\_Aur\_Shabnam\_(1992\_film) "Shola Aur Shabnam (1992 film)")_ (1992), _[Lootere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lootere "Lootere")_ (1993), _[Waqt Hamara Hai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waqt\_Hamara\_Hai "Waqt Hamara Hai")_ (1993), _[Khalnayak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalnayak "Khalnayak")_ (1993), _[Hum Hain Kamaal Ke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hum\_Hain\_Kamaal\_Ke "Hum Hain Kamaal Ke")_ (1993), _[Gumrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gumrah\_(1993\_film) "Gumrah (1993 film)")_ (1993) and _[Darr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darr "Darr")_ (1993).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-Filmography-51) He then appeared in [Sooraj Barjatya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sooraj_Barjatya "Sooraj Barjatya")'s _[Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hum\_Aapke\_Hain\_Koun..! "Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!")_ (1994) and [Aditya Chopra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aditya_Chopra "Aditya Chopra")'s _[Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilwale\_Dulhania\_Le\_Jayenge "Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge")_ (1995).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-toi800-52) Both the films did extremely well at the box office and emerged _All Time Blockbusters_ as well as the highest and second highest-grossing film of all time, respectively.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-54) For his performance in the former, Kher received another nomination in the [Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor "Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor") category.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-Film-55) In the late-1990s, he continued to play supporting roles commercially successful ventures, such as _[Judwaa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judwaa "Judwaa")_ (1997), _[Ziddi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ziddi\_(1997\_film) "Ziddi (1997 film)")_ (1997), _[Deewana Mastana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deewana\_Mastana "Deewana Mastana")_ (1997), _[Kuch Kuch Hota Hai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuch\_Kuch\_Hota\_Hai "Kuch Kuch Hota Hai")_ (1998), _[Bade Miyan Chote Miyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bade\_Miyan\_Chote\_Miyan\_(1998\_film) "Bade Miyan Chote Miyan (1998 film)")_ (1998), _[Hum Aapke Dil Mein Rehte Hain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hum\_Aapke\_Dil\_Mein\_Rehte\_Hain "Hum Aapke Dil Mein Rehte Hain")_ (1999) and _[Haseena Maan Jaayegi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haseena\_Maan\_Jaayegi "Haseena Maan Jaayegi")_ (1999).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-Filmography-51)

Kher began the new decade playing an antagonist in [Rakesh Roshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rakesh_Roshan "Rakesh Roshan")'s [romantic blockbuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_film "Romance film")_[Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaho\_Naa...\_Pyaar\_Hai "Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai")_ which made [Hrithik Roshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hrithik_Roshan "Hrithik Roshan") a star.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-57) He followed it with four more major successes the same year with _[Dulhan Hum Le Jayenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulhan\_Hum\_Le\_Jayenge "Dulhan Hum Le Jayenge")_, _[Kya Kehna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kya\_Kehna "Kya Kehna")_, _[Hamara Dil Aapke Paas Hai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamara\_Dil\_Aapke\_Paas\_Hai "Hamara Dil Aapke Paas Hai")_ and _[Mohabbatein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohabbatein "Mohabbatein")_.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-Filmography-51) In 2001, he had another hit in _[Jodi No.1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jodi\_No.1\_(film) "Jodi No.1 (film)")_ and received praise for his performance in _[Rehnaa Hai Terre Dil Mein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehnaa\_Hai\_Terre\_Dil\_Mein "Rehnaa Hai Terre Dil Mein")_, which did not do well commercially, but went on to attain cult status in later years.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-Filmography-51)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-58)

### Expansion to Hollywood and further acclaim (2002–2018)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anupam_Kher&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Expansion to Hollywood and further acclaim (2002–2018)")]

In 2002, Kher starred in his first [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States") project which was [Gurinder Chadha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurinder_Chadha "Gurinder Chadha")'s [sports comedy drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_film "Sport film")_[Bend It Like Beckham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bend\_It\_Like\_Beckham "Bend It Like Beckham")_.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-59) The film proved to be a critical and commercial success grossing around $76.6 million worldwide.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-61) A year later, he reunited with Chadha for _[Bride and Prejudice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bride\_and\_Prejudice "Bride and Prejudice")_, which too was a successful venture.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-62) His final collaboration with Chadha took place in 2005 for _[The Mistress of Spices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mistress\_of\_Spices "The Mistress of Spices")_, which had [Aishwarya Rai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aishwarya_Rai "Aishwarya Rai") and [Dylan McDermott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_McDermott "Dylan McDermott") in the lead and unlike their previous ventures was panned by critics and did not do well.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-64)

During this period, Kher continued to star in notable Hindi films, such as _[Veer-Zaara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veer-Zaara "Veer-Zaara")_ (2004), _[Kyaa Kool Hain Hum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyaa\_Kool\_Hain\_Hum "Kyaa Kool Hain Hum")_ (2005) and received immense acclaim and his second [National Film Award – Special Jury Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Award_%E2%80%93_Special_Jury_Award_(feature_film) "National Film Award – Special Jury Award (feature film)") for the 2005 film _[Maine Gandhi Ko Nahin Mara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine\_Gandhi\_Ko\_Nahin\_Mara "Maine Gandhi Ko Nahin Mara")_ (which he also produced).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-Filmography-51)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-auto-65) In the latter-half of the 2000s, he appeared in critically and commercially successful [Bollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bollywood "Bollywood") films, including _[Rang De Basanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rang\_De\_Basanti "Rang De Basanti")_ (2006), _[Chup Chup Ke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chup\_Chup\_Ke "Chup Chup Ke")_ (2006), _[Vivah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivah "Vivah")_ (2006), _[Khosla Ka Ghosla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khosla\_Ka\_Ghosla "Khosla Ka Ghosla")_ (2006), _[Apna Sapna Money Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apna\_Sapna\_Money\_Money "Apna Sapna Money Money")_ (2006), _[A Wednesday!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Wednesday! "A Wednesday!")_ (2008), _[Wake Up Sid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake\_Up\_Sid "Wake Up Sid")_ (2009) and made his [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_China "Cinema of China") film debut with _[Lust, Caution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lust,\_Caution "Lust, Caution")_ (2007), which too was a box office hit grossing around $67.1 million.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-66)

In the following decade, Kher did films of varied genres and found box office success in _[Dabangg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dabangg "Dabangg")_ (2010), _[Yamla Pagla Deewana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamla\_Pagla\_Deewana "Yamla Pagla Deewana")_ (2011), _[Kya Super Kool Hain Hum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kya\_Super\_Kool\_Hain\_Hum "Kya Super Kool Hain Hum")_ (2012), _[Chashme Baddoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chashme\_Baddoor\_(2013\_film) "Chashme Baddoor (2013 film)")_ (2013), _[Singham Returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singham\_Returns "Singham Returns")_ (2014), _[Prem Ratan Dhan Payo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prem\_Ratan\_Dhan\_Payo "Prem Ratan Dhan Payo")_ (2015), _[M.S. Dhoni: The Untold Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M.S.\_Dhoni:\_The\_Untold\_Story "M.S. Dhoni: The Untold Story")_ (2016), _[Toilet: Ek Prem Katha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toilet:\_Ek\_Prem\_Katha "Toilet: Ek Prem Katha")_ (2017) and _[Judwaa 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judwaa\_2 "Judwaa 2")_ (2017).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-Filmography-51) He also received praise for his performances in _[Special 26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special\_26 "Special 26")_ (2013), _[Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby\_(2015\_Hindi\_film) "Baby (2015 Hindi film)")_ (2015), _[Indu Sarkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indu\_Sarkar "Indu Sarkar")_ (2017) and _[Love Sonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love\_Sonia "Love Sonia")_ (2018). For _Special 26_, he received a nomination in the Best Supporting Actor category at [59th Filmfare Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/59th_Filmfare_Awards "59th Filmfare Awards").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-67) During this period, he also made his [Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam "Malayalam") film debut with [Blessy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blessy "Blessy")'s _[Pranayam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pranayam\_(2011\_film) "Pranayam (2011 film)")_ (2011), played supporting roles in blockbuster Hollywood ventures, including [David O. Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_O._Russell "David O. Russell")'s _[Silver Linings Playbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver\_Linings\_Playbook "Silver Linings Playbook")_ (2012) and [Michael Showalter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Showalter "Michael Showalter")'s _[The Big Sick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Big\_Sick "The Big Sick")_ (2017) and received a nomination in the [BAFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA "BAFTA")[Best Supporting Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_Television_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor "British Academy Television Award for Best Supporting Actor") category for his performance in Lynsey Miller's _[The Boy With The Topknot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boy\_With\_The\_Topknot "The Boy With The Topknot")_ (2017).[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-70)

### Work in regional industries and continued success (2019–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anupam_Kher&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Work in regional industries and continued success (2019–present)")]

In 2019, Kher played the role of former [PM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister "Prime Minister")[Manmohan Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manmohan_Singh "Manmohan Singh") in _[The Accidental Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Accidental\_Prime\_Minister\_(film) "The Accidental Prime Minister (film)")_ and a vigilante in _[One Day: Justice Delivered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One\_Day:\_Justice\_Delivered "One Day: Justice Delivered")_, both of which were critical and commercial failures.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-72)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-Filmography-51) After a gap of almost 3 years, he returned to the big screen playing one of the leads in [Vivek Agnihotri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivek_Agnihotri "Vivek Agnihotri")'s _[The Kashmir Files](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kashmir\_Files "The Kashmir Files")_ (2022). It received polarising response from critics, but proved to be a huge blockbuster and got Kher a nomination in the Best Actor category at [68th Filmfare Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/68th_Filmfare_Awards "68th Filmfare Awards").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-Filmography-51)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-73) The same year he appeared in the [Telugu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telugu_language "Telugu language") film _[Karthikeya 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karthikeya\_2 "Karthikeya 2")_, which also emerged a blockbuster at the box office.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-74)

In 2023, he appeared in the successful Malayalam comedy _[Voice of Sathyanathan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice\_of\_Sathyanathan "Voice of Sathyanathan")_ and [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada") actioner _[Ghost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost\_(2023\_film) "Ghost (2023 film)")_, which too did well.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-76) This was followed by a series of box office duds like _[Shiv Shastri Balboa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiv\_Shastri\_Balboa "Shiv Shastri Balboa")_ (2023), _[IB71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IB71 "IB71")_ (2023), _[The Vaccine War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Vaccine\_War "The Vaccine War")_ (2023), _[Emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency\_(2025\_film) "Emergency (2025 film)")_ (2025) and _[Tumko Meri Kasam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumko\_Meri\_Kasam "Tumko Meri Kasam")_ (2025) with the exception being [Anurag Basu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anurag_Basu "Anurag Basu")'s romantic musical _[Metro In Dino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro\_In\_Dino "Metro In Dino")_ (2025) for which Kher also made his playback debut.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-79)

## Other works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anupam_Kher&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Other works")]

Kher ventured into directing with _[Om Jai Jagadish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Om\_Jai\_Jagadish "Om Jai Jagadish")_ (2002) and has been a producer. He produced and starred in the film _[Maine Gandhi Ko Nahin Mara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine\_Gandhi\_Ko\_Nahin\_Mara "Maine Gandhi Ko Nahin Mara")_ (2005). From October 2003 to October 2004, he served as chairman of the [Indian Film Censor Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Board_of_Film_Certification "Central Board of Film Certification").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-80)

In 2011 Kher released his first book _The Best Thing About You is You!_, which was a best-seller. His biography _Lessons Life Taught Me Unknowingly_ was published on 5 August 2019 by [Penguin Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Random_House "Penguin Random House"). In 2020, he wrote _Your Best Day Is Today!_, based on his experiences of the [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") crisis.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-84) Remembering his father on his 9th [death anniversary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_anniversary "Death anniversary"), he presented a poem written by [Lucknow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucknow "Lucknow")-based poet [Pankaj Prasun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pankaj_Prasun "Pankaj Prasun") and posted it on social media.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-85)

Kher hosted TV shows such as _Say Na Something To Anupam Uncle_, _[Sawaal Dus Crore Ka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sawaal\_Dus\_Crore\_Ka "Sawaal Dus Crore Ka")_ and _[Lead India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead\_India "Lead India")_. In 2014, Kher has written and starred in a play about his own life called _[Kucch Bhi Ho Sakta Hai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Anupam\_Kher\_Show\_%E2%80%93\_Kucch\_Bhi\_Ho\_Sakta\_Hai "The Anupam Kher Show – Kucch Bhi Ho Sakta Hai")_, which was directed by [Feroz Abbas Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feroz_Abbas_Khan "Feroz Abbas Khan").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-KBHSH-25)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-86) In 2016, Anupam Kher was a narrator in the [ABP News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABP_News "ABP News") documentary TV series _[Bharatvarsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharatvarsh\_(TV\_series) "Bharatvarsh (TV series)")_,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-88) which showcased the journey from [ancient India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outline_of_ancient_India "Outline of ancient India") to the 19th century.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-89)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-91) In late 2016, Anupam Kher produced _[Khwaabon Ki Zamin Par](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khwaabon\_Ki\_Zamin\_Par "Khwaabon Ki Zamin Par")_, a TV drama airing on [Zindagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zindagi_(TV_channel) "Zindagi (TV channel)").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-92)

Starting in fall of 2018, Anupam Kher starred in NBC medical drama TV series _[New Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Amsterdam\_(2018\_TV\_series) "New Amsterdam (2018 TV series)")_[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-93) as Dr. Vijay Kapoor (a neurologist). He also appeared as Shahbaz Karim in the [BBC1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC1 "BBC1") drama _[Mrs Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrs\_Wilson "Mrs Wilson")_.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-94) Kher is the founder of Actor Prepares, an acting institute based in Mumbai.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-95)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anupam_Kher&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Kher married actress Madhumati Kapoor in 1979, but divorced after a few years.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-96) In 1985, he married actress [Kirron Kher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirron_Kher "Kirron Kher")[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-97) who is a [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament,_Lok_Sabha "Member of Parliament, Lok Sabha") from [Chandigarh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandigarh "Chandigarh"), belonging to the [BJP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BJP "BJP").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-98)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-TOI-99) Her son, his stepson, is actor [Sikandar Kher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikandar_Kher "Sikandar Kher").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-100) In 2010, he was appointed as the goodwill ambassador of the [Pratham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratham "Pratham") Education Foundation, which strives to improve children's education in India.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-Anupam_Kher_tells_us_about_his_new_role-101) Kher is an ardent supporter of the [Bharatiya Janata Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharatiya_Janata_Party "Bharatiya Janata Party") (BJP) and Indian prime minister [Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi "Narendra Modi").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-:3-14)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-102)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-103)

On 20 September 2021, Kher was awarded an [honorary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_degree "Honorary degree")[doctorate degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctorate_degree "Doctorate degree") in [Philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy") of [Hindu Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_Studies "Hindu Studies") by the [Hindu University of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_University_of_America "Hindu University of America").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupam_Kher#cite_note-104)

**Girish Raghunath Kārnād** (19 May 1938 – 10 June 2019)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-TNM-1) was an Indian playwright, actor, film director, writer,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-2) and a [Jnanpith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jnanpith_Award "Jnanpith Award") awardee, who predominantly worked in [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada"), [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi"), [Tamil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamil_language "Tamil language"), [Telugu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telugu_language "Telugu language"), [Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam "Malayalam") and [Marathi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathi_language "Marathi language") films. His rise as a playwright in the 1960s marked the coming of age of modern Indian playwriting in Kannada, just as [Badal Sarkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badal_Sarkar "Badal Sarkar") did in Bengali, [Vijay Tendulkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijay_Tendulkar "Vijay Tendulkar") in Marathi, and [Mohan Rakesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohan_Rakesh "Mohan Rakesh") in Hindi.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-3) He was a recipient of the 1998 [Jnanpith Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jnanpith_Award "Jnanpith Award"), the highest literary honour conferred in India.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-4)

For four decades Karnad composed plays, often using history and mythology to tackle contemporary issues. He translated his plays into English and received acclaim. His plays have been translated into some Indian languages and directed by directors like [Ebrahim Alkazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebrahim_Alkazi "Ebrahim Alkazi"), [B. V. Karanth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._V._Karanth "B. V. Karanth"), [Alyque Padamsee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alyque_Padamsee "Alyque Padamsee"), [Prasanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prasanna_(theatre_director) "Prasanna (theatre director)"), [Arvind Gaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arvind_Gaur "Arvind Gaur"), [Satyadev Dubey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyadev_Dubey "Satyadev Dubey"), [Vijaya Mehta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijaya_Mehta "Vijaya Mehta"), [Shyamanand Jalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shyamanand_Jalan "Shyamanand Jalan"), Amal Allanaa and Zafer Mohiuddin.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5)

He was active in the world of Indian cinema working as an actor, director and screenwriter, in Hindi and Kannada cinema, and has earned awards.

He was conferred [Padma Shri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Shri "Padma Shri") and [Padma Bhushan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Bhushan "Padma Bhushan") by the Government of India and won four [Filmfare Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Awards_South "Filmfare Awards South"), of which three are Filmfare Award for Best Director – Kannada and the fourth a Filmfare Best Screenplay Award. He was a presenter for a weekly science magazine programme called "Turning Point" that aired on [Doordarshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doordarshan "Doordarshan") in 1991.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Girish Karnad was born in a [Konkani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konkani_language "Konkani language")-speaking [Chitrapur Saraswat Brahmin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chitrapur_Saraswat_Brahmin "Chitrapur Saraswat Brahmin") family of [Matheran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matheran "Matheran"), in present-day [Maharashtra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharashtra "Maharashtra"), in 1938.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-6) His mother Krishnabai (née Mankikar) was a young widow with a son who belonged to a poor family. Since it was necessary for her to earn a living, she began working as a nurse and cook (general housekeeper) for the bedridden wife of a certain Raghunath Karnad, a doctor in the [Bombay Medical Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombay_Medical_Services "Bombay Medical Services").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-7)

Some five years later, and while the first wife was still alive, Krishnabai and Raghunath Karnad were married in a private ceremony. The marriage was controversial not because of bigamy (it was legal until 1956 for a Hindu man to have more than one wife) but because of the prevailing social prejudice against widow remarriage. Therefore, the wedding was held privately, and under the dispensation of the [Arya Samaj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arya_Samaj "Arya Samaj"), a reform organization that condones widow remarriage. Girish was the third of the four children born thereafter.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-8)

Karnad's initial schooling was in Marathi. Later, after his father was transferred to [Sirsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirsi,_Karnataka "Sirsi, Karnataka") in the [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada")-speaking regions of [Bombay Presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombay_Presidency "Bombay Presidency"), Karnad was exposed to travelling theatre groups and _nataka mandalis_ (theatre troupes), which were experiencing a period of efflorescence during the iconic [Balgandharva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balgandharva "Balgandharva") era .[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-9) As a youngster, he was an ardent admirer of [Yakshagana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakshagana "Yakshagana") and the theater in his village.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-interview-10) His family moved to [Dharwad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharwad "Dharwad") in Karnataka when he was fourteen, where he grew up with his two sisters and a niece.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-mint-11)

After completing his schooling at the Basel Mission Boys School, Dharwad,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-12) he earned his [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") degree in mathematics and statistics from Karnataka Arts College, [Dharwad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharwad "Dharwad") ([Karnataka University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnataka_University "Karnataka University")), in 1958. After graduation, he went to England and studied philosophy, Politics and Economics at [Magdalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalen_College,_Oxford "Magdalen College, Oxford") in [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") as a [Rhodes Scholar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Scholar "Rhodes Scholar") (1960–63), earning his [Master of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Arts "Master of Arts") degree in philosophy, [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science") and economics.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5) Karnad was elected the President of the [Oxford Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Union "Oxford Union") in 1962–63.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hibbert-13)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

After working with the [Oxford University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University_Press "Oxford University Press"), Chennai for seven years (1963–70), he resigned to take to writing full-time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5) While in Madras (now known as Chennai) he got involved with local amateur theatre group, [The Madras Players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Madras_Players "The Madras Players").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-14)

During 1987–88, he was at the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago") as visiting professor and [Fulbright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulbright "Fulbright") playwright-in-residence.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5) During his tenure at Chicago _Nagamandala_ had its world premiere at the [Guthrie Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guthrie_Theater "Guthrie Theater") in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") based on Karnad's English translation of the Kannada original.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-today-15)

He served as director of the [Film and Television Institute of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_and_Television_Institute_of_India "Film and Television Institute of India") (1974–1975) and chairman of the [Sangeet Natak Akademi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangeet_Natak_Akademi "Sangeet Natak Akademi"), the national academy of the performing arts (1988–93). He served as director of the Nehru Centre and as Minister of Culture, in the Indian High Commission, London (2000–2003).

### Literature

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Literature")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Girish-Karnad.jpg/250px-Girish-Karnad.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Girish-Karnad.jpg)

Karnad in 2010

Karnad is known as a playwright. His plays, written in [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada"), have been translated into English (mostly translated by himself) and some Indian languages. Kannada is his language of choice.

When Karnad started writing plays, [Kannada literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada_literature "Kannada literature") was highly influenced by the renaissance in [Western literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_literature "Western literature"). Writers would choose a subject that looked entirely alien to manifestation of native soil. [C. Rajagopalachari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Rajagopalachari "C. Rajagopalachari")'s version of the _[Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata")_ published in 1951, left a deep impact on him[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-sachi58-16) and soon, sometime in the mid-1950s, one day he experienced a rush of dialogues by characters from the Mahabharata in Kannada.

"I could actually hear the dialogues being spoken into my ears ... I was just the scribe," said Karnad in a later interview. _Yayati_ was published in 1961, when he was 23 years old. It is based on the story of King [Yayati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yayati "Yayati"), one of the ancestors of the [Pandavas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandavas "Pandavas"), who was cursed into premature old age by his preceptor, [Shukracharya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shukracharya "Shukracharya"), who was incensed at Yayati's infidelity.

Yayati, in turn, asks his sons to sacrifice their youth for him, and one of them agrees. It ridicules the ironies of life through characters in _Mahabharata_. The play in Hindi was adapted by [Satyadev Dubey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyadev_Dubey "Satyadev Dubey") and [Amrish Puri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrish_Puri "Amrish Puri") was lead actor for the play. It became an instant success, immediately translated and staged in several other Indian languages.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-today-15)

Karnad found a new approach of drawing historical and mythological sources to tackle contemporary themes and [existentialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existentialist "Existentialist") crisis of modern man through characters locked in psychological and philosophical conflicts. His next was _[Tughlaq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tughlaq\_(play) "Tughlaq (play)")_ (1964), about a rashly idealist 14th-century [Sultan of Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_of_Delhi "Sultan of Delhi"), [Muhammad bin Tughluq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_bin_Tughluq "Muhammad bin Tughluq"), and allegory on the [Nehruvian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru "Jawaharlal Nehru") era which started with ambitious idealism and ended up in disillusionment.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-sachi58-16) This established Karnad, now 26 years old, as a promising playwright in the [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"). It was staged by the [National School of Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_School_of_Drama "National School of Drama") Repertory under the direction of [Ebrahim Alkazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebrahim_Alkazi "Ebrahim Alkazi"), with the actor [Manohar Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manohar_Singh "Manohar Singh"), playing the visionary king who later becomes disillusioned and turns bitter, amidst the historic [Purana Qila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purana_Qila "Purana Qila") in Delhi. It was staged in London by the National School of Drama for the Festival of India in 1982.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-today-15)

_[Hayavadana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayavadana "Hayavadana")_ (1971) was based on a theme drawn from _The Transposed Heads_, a 1940 novella by [Thomas Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Mann "Thomas Mann"), which is originally found in the 11th-century Sanskrit text _[Kathasaritsagara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathasaritsagara "Kathasaritsagara")_. Herein he employed the folk theatre form of [Yakshagana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakshagana "Yakshagana"). A German version of the play was directed by [Vijaya Mehta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijaya_Mehta "Vijaya Mehta") as part of the repertoire of the [Deutsches National Theatre, Weimar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsches_Nationaltheater_and_Staatskapelle_Weimar "Deutsches Nationaltheater and Staatskapelle Weimar").

_Naga-Mandala_ (Play with Cobra, 1988) was based on a folk tale related to him by A. K. Ramanujam, brought him the Karnataka Sahitya Academy Award for the Most Creative Work of 1989. It was directed by J. Garland Wright, as part of the celebrations of the 30th anniversary of Guthrie Theatre, Minneapolis. The theatre subsequently commissioned him to write the play, _Agni Mattu Male_ (The Fire and the Rain). Though before it came _[Taledanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taledanda "Taledanda")_ (Death by Beheading, 1990) which used the backdrop, the rise of [Veerashaivism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veerashaivism "Veerashaivism"), a radical protest and reform movement in 12th century Karnataka to bring out current issues.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-17)

### Movies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Movies")]

Karnad made his acting as well as screenwriting debut in a Kannada movie, _[Samskara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samskara\_(film) "Samskara (film)")_ (1970), based on a novel by [U.R. Ananthamurthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.R._Ananthamurthy "U.R. Ananthamurthy") and directed by Pattabhirama Reddy. That movie won the first [President's Golden Lotus Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Award_for_Best_Feature_Film "National Film Award for Best Feature Film") for [Kannada cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_Karnataka "Cinema of Karnataka").

In television, he played the role of Swami's father in the TV series _[Malgudi Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgudi\_Days\_(TV\_series) "Malgudi Days (TV series)")_ (1986–1987), based on [R. K. Narayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._K._Narayan "R. K. Narayan")'s books, directed by [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada") actor and director [Shankar Nag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shankar_Nag "Shankar Nag"). He also hosted the science magazine [Turning Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turning_Point_(Doordarshan) "Turning Point (Doordarshan)") on Doordarshan, in the early 1990s.

He made his directorial debut with _[Vamsha Vriksha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vamsha\_Vriksha "Vamsha Vriksha")_ (1971), based on a [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada") novel by [S. L. Bhyrappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S._L._Bhyrappa "S. L. Bhyrappa"). It won him [National Film Award for Best Direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Award_for_Best_Direction "National Film Award for Best Direction") along with [B. V. Karanth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._V._Karanth "B. V. Karanth"), who co-directed the film. Later, Karnad directed several movies in [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada") and [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi"), including _[Godhuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godhuli "Godhuli")_ (1977), _[Utsav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utsav "Utsav")_ (1984) and _[Cheluvi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheluvi "Cheluvi")_ (1992). Karnad has made number of documentaries, like one on the Kannada poet [D. R. Bendre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D._R._Bendre "D. R. Bendre") (1972), _Kanaka-Purandara_ (English, 1988) on two medieval [Bhakti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhakti "Bhakti") poets of Karnataka, [Kanaka Dasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanaka_Dasa "Kanaka Dasa") and [Purandara Dasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purandara_Dasa "Purandara Dasa"), and _The Lamp in the Niche_ (English, 1989) on Sufism and the [Bhakti movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhakti_movement "Bhakti movement"). Many of his films and documentaries have won several national and international awards.

Some of his famous Kannada movies include _[Tabbaliyu Neenade Magane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabbaliyu\_Neenade\_Magane "Tabbaliyu Neenade Magane")_, _[Ondanondu Kaladalli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ondanondu\_Kaladalli "Ondanondu Kaladalli")_ and _[Kaadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaadu\_(1973\_Kannada\_film) "Kaadu (1973 Kannada film)")_ and most recent film _Kanooru Heggaditi_ (1999), based on a novel by Kannada writer [Kuvempu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuvempu "Kuvempu").

His Hindi movies include _[Nishaant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nishaant "Nishaant")_ (1975), _[Manthan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manthan "Manthan")_ (1976), _[Swami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swami\_(1977\_film) "Swami (1977 film)")_ (1977), and _[Pukar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pukar\_(2000\_film) "Pukar (2000 film)")_ (2000). He has acted in a number of [Nagesh Kukunoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagesh_Kukunoor "Nagesh Kukunoor") films, starting with _[Iqbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iqbal\_(film) "Iqbal (film)")_ (2005), where Karnad's role of the ruthless cricket coach got him critical acclaim. This was followed by _[Dor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dor\_(film) "Dor (film)")_ (2006), _[8 x 10 Tasveer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8\_x\_10\_Tasveer "8 x 10 Tasveer")_ (2009) and _[Aashayein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aashayein "Aashayein")_ (2010). He played a key role in movies _[Ek Tha Tiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ek\_Tha\_Tiger "Ek Tha Tiger")_ (2012) and its sequel _[Tiger Zinda Hai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger\_Zinda\_Hai "Tiger Zinda Hai")_ (2017) produced by [Yash Raj Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yash_Raj_Films "Yash Raj Films").

Karnad has acted in the Kannada gangster movie _[Aa Dinagalu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aa\_Dinagalu "Aa Dinagalu")_.

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Controversies")]

At the Tata Literary Festival held in [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai") in 2012, Karnad was invited to speak about "his life in theater" in an hour-long session. During his speech, he lashed out at [V. S. Naipaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul "V. S. Naipaul") for his "antipathy towards Indian Muslims". Naipaul had earlier been conferred the Lifetime achievement award by the festival's organisers. Karnad also criticized the organizers for having honored Naipaul. The audience, which had gathered to hear Karnad speak, had mixed reactions to the speech. Some, like organizer [Anil Dharker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anil_Dharker "Anil Dharker"), tried ineffectually to steer the speech toward less controversial waters. Others were amused by the episode, and some commented on the research and logic that had gone into the speech (unfortunately overshadowed by its 'scandalous' nature).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-ie-24)

Just a few weeks after this, Karnad again created controversy by claiming that [Rabindranath Tagore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore "Rabindranath Tagore"), who wrote India's national anthem, was a great poet but a second-rate playwright.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-dc-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-26)

In November 2015, during celebrations marking the anniversary of 18th-century Muslim ruler [Tipu Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipu_Sultan "Tipu Sultan")'s birth, Karnad stated that [Bangalore International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kempegowda_International_Airport "Kempegowda International Airport") should have been named after Tipu Sultan instead of [Kempe Gowda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kempe_Gowda_I "Kempe Gowda I"). This created a furore among many people. Karnad apologised the following day.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-28)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Personal life")]

While working in Madras for Oxford University Press on his return from England, Karnad met his future wife Saraswathi Ganapathy at a party. They decided to marry but the marriage was only formalised ten years later, when Karnad was 42 years old. Saraswathi was born to a [Parsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsi "Parsi") mother, Nurgesh Mugaseth, and a [Kodava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodava_people "Kodava people") Hindu father, Kodandera Ganapathy.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-ourkarnataka-29) The couple had two children. They lived in [Bengaluru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengaluru "Bengaluru").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5) He was extremely fluent and well-versed in [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada"), [Konkani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konkani_language "Konkani language"), [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi"), [Marathi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathi_(language) "Marathi (language)"), and English.

## Activism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Activism")]

He was a proponent of multiculturalism and freedom of expression. He was a critic of [religious fundamentalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_fundamentalism "Religious fundamentalism"). He had publicly condemned the [demolition of Babri Masjid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demolition_of_Babri_Masjid "Demolition of Babri Masjid") in 1992 and later spoke against the attempts to create [controversy about the Idgah Maidan in Hubli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubli_Idgah_Maidan_dispute "Hubli Idgah Maidan dispute").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5) He had opposed [RSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashtriya_Swayamsevak_Sangh "Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh"), [BJP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BJP "BJP") and other organizations on several occasions. He opposed [Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi "Narendra Modi") for the Prime Minister's post in the [2014 parliament elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Indian_general_election "2014 Indian general election").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-:0-30) He was one of the 200 writers who put out an open letter against hate politics and for “diverse and equal India” during the 2019 general elections. With a tube in his nose, he wore a placard saying "Me Too Urban Naxal"[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-31) at the first death anniversary of slain journalist [Gauri Lankesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauri_Lankesh "Gauri Lankesh").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-:0-30) Karnad claimed that [Tipu Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipu_Sultan "Tipu Sultan") was the greatest king Karnataka had in 500 years, on a religious controversy about the king.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-:0-30) Karnad was a supporter of the Forum for Communal Harmony.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-32)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Death")]

Karnad died on 10 June 2019 at Bengaluru at the age of 81 due to multiple organ failure following prolonged illness.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-33) "After a discussion with his son, it was made clear to us that his last wish was to not have any floral procession, VVIPs or visits of any dignitaries. Hence, it will be a simple affair."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-34)

**Girish Raghunath Kārnād** (19 May 1938 – 10 June 2019)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-TNM-1) was an Indian playwright, actor, film director, writer,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-2) and a [Jnanpith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jnanpith_Award "Jnanpith Award") awardee, who predominantly worked in [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada"), [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi"), [Tamil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamil_language "Tamil language"), [Telugu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telugu_language "Telugu language"), [Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam "Malayalam") and [Marathi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathi_language "Marathi language") films. His rise as a playwright in the 1960s marked the coming of age of modern Indian playwriting in Kannada, just as [Badal Sarkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badal_Sarkar "Badal Sarkar") did in Bengali, [Vijay Tendulkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijay_Tendulkar "Vijay Tendulkar") in Marathi, and [Mohan Rakesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohan_Rakesh "Mohan Rakesh") in Hindi.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-3) He was a recipient of the 1998 [Jnanpith Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jnanpith_Award "Jnanpith Award"), the highest literary honour conferred in India.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-4)

For four decades Karnad composed plays, often using history and mythology to tackle contemporary issues. He translated his plays into English and received acclaim. His plays have been translated into some Indian languages and directed by directors like [Ebrahim Alkazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebrahim_Alkazi "Ebrahim Alkazi"), [B. V. Karanth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._V._Karanth "B. V. Karanth"), [Alyque Padamsee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alyque_Padamsee "Alyque Padamsee"), [Prasanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prasanna_(theatre_director) "Prasanna (theatre director)"), [Arvind Gaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arvind_Gaur "Arvind Gaur"), [Satyadev Dubey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyadev_Dubey "Satyadev Dubey"), [Vijaya Mehta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijaya_Mehta "Vijaya Mehta"), [Shyamanand Jalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shyamanand_Jalan "Shyamanand Jalan"), Amal Allanaa and Zafer Mohiuddin.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5)

He was active in the world of Indian cinema working as an actor, director and screenwriter, in Hindi and Kannada cinema, and has earned awards.

He was conferred [Padma Shri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Shri "Padma Shri") and [Padma Bhushan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Bhushan "Padma Bhushan") by the Government of India and won four [Filmfare Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmfare_Awards_South "Filmfare Awards South"), of which three are Filmfare Award for Best Director – Kannada and the fourth a Filmfare Best Screenplay Award. He was a presenter for a weekly science magazine programme called "Turning Point" that aired on [Doordarshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doordarshan "Doordarshan") in 1991.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Girish Karnad was born in a [Konkani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konkani_language "Konkani language")-speaking [Chitrapur Saraswat Brahmin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chitrapur_Saraswat_Brahmin "Chitrapur Saraswat Brahmin") family of [Matheran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matheran "Matheran"), in present-day [Maharashtra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharashtra "Maharashtra"), in 1938.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-6) His mother Krishnabai (née Mankikar) was a young widow with a son who belonged to a poor family. Since it was necessary for her to earn a living, she began working as a nurse and cook (general housekeeper) for the bedridden wife of a certain Raghunath Karnad, a doctor in the [Bombay Medical Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombay_Medical_Services "Bombay Medical Services").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-7)

Some five years later, and while the first wife was still alive, Krishnabai and Raghunath Karnad were married in a private ceremony. The marriage was controversial not because of bigamy (it was legal until 1956 for a Hindu man to have more than one wife) but because of the prevailing social prejudice against widow remarriage. Therefore, the wedding was held privately, and under the dispensation of the [Arya Samaj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arya_Samaj "Arya Samaj"), a reform organization that condones widow remarriage. Girish was the third of the four children born thereafter.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-8)

Karnad's initial schooling was in Marathi. Later, after his father was transferred to [Sirsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirsi,_Karnataka "Sirsi, Karnataka") in the [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada")-speaking regions of [Bombay Presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombay_Presidency "Bombay Presidency"), Karnad was exposed to travelling theatre groups and _nataka mandalis_ (theatre troupes), which were experiencing a period of efflorescence during the iconic [Balgandharva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balgandharva "Balgandharva") era .[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-9) As a youngster, he was an ardent admirer of [Yakshagana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakshagana "Yakshagana") and the theater in his village.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-interview-10) His family moved to [Dharwad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharwad "Dharwad") in Karnataka when he was fourteen, where he grew up with his two sisters and a niece.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-mint-11)

After completing his schooling at the Basel Mission Boys School, Dharwad,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-12) he earned his [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") degree in mathematics and statistics from Karnataka Arts College, [Dharwad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharwad "Dharwad") ([Karnataka University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnataka_University "Karnataka University")), in 1958. After graduation, he went to England and studied philosophy, Politics and Economics at [Magdalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalen_College,_Oxford "Magdalen College, Oxford") in [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") as a [Rhodes Scholar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Scholar "Rhodes Scholar") (1960–63), earning his [Master of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Arts "Master of Arts") degree in philosophy, [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science") and economics.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5) Karnad was elected the President of the [Oxford Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Union "Oxford Union") in 1962–63.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hibbert-13)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

After working with the [Oxford University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University_Press "Oxford University Press"), Chennai for seven years (1963–70), he resigned to take to writing full-time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5) While in Madras (now known as Chennai) he got involved with local amateur theatre group, [The Madras Players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Madras_Players "The Madras Players").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-14)

During 1987–88, he was at the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago") as visiting professor and [Fulbright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulbright "Fulbright") playwright-in-residence.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5) During his tenure at Chicago _Nagamandala_ had its world premiere at the [Guthrie Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guthrie_Theater "Guthrie Theater") in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") based on Karnad's English translation of the Kannada original.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-today-15)

He served as director of the [Film and Television Institute of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_and_Television_Institute_of_India "Film and Television Institute of India") (1974–1975) and chairman of the [Sangeet Natak Akademi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangeet_Natak_Akademi "Sangeet Natak Akademi"), the national academy of the performing arts (1988–93). He served as director of the Nehru Centre and as Minister of Culture, in the Indian High Commission, London (2000–2003).

### Literature

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Literature")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Girish-Karnad.jpg/250px-Girish-Karnad.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Girish-Karnad.jpg)

Karnad in 2010

Karnad is known as a playwright. His plays, written in [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada"), have been translated into English (mostly translated by himself) and some Indian languages. Kannada is his language of choice.

When Karnad started writing plays, [Kannada literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada_literature "Kannada literature") was highly influenced by the renaissance in [Western literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_literature "Western literature"). Writers would choose a subject that looked entirely alien to manifestation of native soil. [C. Rajagopalachari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Rajagopalachari "C. Rajagopalachari")'s version of the _[Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata")_ published in 1951, left a deep impact on him[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-sachi58-16) and soon, sometime in the mid-1950s, one day he experienced a rush of dialogues by characters from the Mahabharata in Kannada.

"I could actually hear the dialogues being spoken into my ears ... I was just the scribe," said Karnad in a later interview. _Yayati_ was published in 1961, when he was 23 years old. It is based on the story of King [Yayati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yayati "Yayati"), one of the ancestors of the [Pandavas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandavas "Pandavas"), who was cursed into premature old age by his preceptor, [Shukracharya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shukracharya "Shukracharya"), who was incensed at Yayati's infidelity.

Yayati, in turn, asks his sons to sacrifice their youth for him, and one of them agrees. It ridicules the ironies of life through characters in _Mahabharata_. The play in Hindi was adapted by [Satyadev Dubey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyadev_Dubey "Satyadev Dubey") and [Amrish Puri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amrish_Puri "Amrish Puri") was lead actor for the play. It became an instant success, immediately translated and staged in several other Indian languages.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-today-15)

Karnad found a new approach of drawing historical and mythological sources to tackle contemporary themes and [existentialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existentialist "Existentialist") crisis of modern man through characters locked in psychological and philosophical conflicts. His next was _[Tughlaq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tughlaq\_(play) "Tughlaq (play)")_ (1964), about a rashly idealist 14th-century [Sultan of Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_of_Delhi "Sultan of Delhi"), [Muhammad bin Tughluq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_bin_Tughluq "Muhammad bin Tughluq"), and allegory on the [Nehruvian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru "Jawaharlal Nehru") era which started with ambitious idealism and ended up in disillusionment.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-sachi58-16) This established Karnad, now 26 years old, as a promising playwright in the [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"). It was staged by the [National School of Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_School_of_Drama "National School of Drama") Repertory under the direction of [Ebrahim Alkazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebrahim_Alkazi "Ebrahim Alkazi"), with the actor [Manohar Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manohar_Singh "Manohar Singh"), playing the visionary king who later becomes disillusioned and turns bitter, amidst the historic [Purana Qila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purana_Qila "Purana Qila") in Delhi. It was staged in London by the National School of Drama for the Festival of India in 1982.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-today-15)

_[Hayavadana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayavadana "Hayavadana")_ (1971) was based on a theme drawn from _The Transposed Heads_, a 1940 novella by [Thomas Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Mann "Thomas Mann"), which is originally found in the 11th-century Sanskrit text _[Kathasaritsagara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathasaritsagara "Kathasaritsagara")_. Herein he employed the folk theatre form of [Yakshagana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakshagana "Yakshagana"). A German version of the play was directed by [Vijaya Mehta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijaya_Mehta "Vijaya Mehta") as part of the repertoire of the [Deutsches National Theatre, Weimar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsches_Nationaltheater_and_Staatskapelle_Weimar "Deutsches Nationaltheater and Staatskapelle Weimar").

_Naga-Mandala_ (Play with Cobra, 1988) was based on a folk tale related to him by A. K. Ramanujam, brought him the Karnataka Sahitya Academy Award for the Most Creative Work of 1989. It was directed by J. Garland Wright, as part of the celebrations of the 30th anniversary of Guthrie Theatre, Minneapolis. The theatre subsequently commissioned him to write the play, _Agni Mattu Male_ (The Fire and the Rain). Though before it came _[Taledanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taledanda "Taledanda")_ (Death by Beheading, 1990) which used the backdrop, the rise of [Veerashaivism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veerashaivism "Veerashaivism"), a radical protest and reform movement in 12th century Karnataka to bring out current issues.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-17)

### Movies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Movies")]

Karnad made his acting as well as screenwriting debut in a Kannada movie, _[Samskara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samskara\_(film) "Samskara (film)")_ (1970), based on a novel by [U.R. Ananthamurthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.R._Ananthamurthy "U.R. Ananthamurthy") and directed by Pattabhirama Reddy. That movie won the first [President's Golden Lotus Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Award_for_Best_Feature_Film "National Film Award for Best Feature Film") for [Kannada cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_Karnataka "Cinema of Karnataka").

In television, he played the role of Swami's father in the TV series _[Malgudi Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malgudi\_Days\_(TV\_series) "Malgudi Days (TV series)")_ (1986–1987), based on [R. K. Narayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._K._Narayan "R. K. Narayan")'s books, directed by [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada") actor and director [Shankar Nag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shankar_Nag "Shankar Nag"). He also hosted the science magazine [Turning Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turning_Point_(Doordarshan) "Turning Point (Doordarshan)") on Doordarshan, in the early 1990s.

He made his directorial debut with _[Vamsha Vriksha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vamsha\_Vriksha "Vamsha Vriksha")_ (1971), based on a [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada") novel by [S. L. Bhyrappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S._L._Bhyrappa "S. L. Bhyrappa"). It won him [National Film Award for Best Direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Award_for_Best_Direction "National Film Award for Best Direction") along with [B. V. Karanth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._V._Karanth "B. V. Karanth"), who co-directed the film. Later, Karnad directed several movies in [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada") and [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi"), including _[Godhuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godhuli "Godhuli")_ (1977), _[Utsav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utsav "Utsav")_ (1984) and _[Cheluvi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheluvi "Cheluvi")_ (1992). Karnad has made number of documentaries, like one on the Kannada poet [D. R. Bendre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D._R._Bendre "D. R. Bendre") (1972), _Kanaka-Purandara_ (English, 1988) on two medieval [Bhakti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhakti "Bhakti") poets of Karnataka, [Kanaka Dasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanaka_Dasa "Kanaka Dasa") and [Purandara Dasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purandara_Dasa "Purandara Dasa"), and _The Lamp in the Niche_ (English, 1989) on Sufism and the [Bhakti movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhakti_movement "Bhakti movement"). Many of his films and documentaries have won several national and international awards.

Some of his famous Kannada movies include _[Tabbaliyu Neenade Magane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabbaliyu\_Neenade\_Magane "Tabbaliyu Neenade Magane")_, _[Ondanondu Kaladalli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ondanondu\_Kaladalli "Ondanondu Kaladalli")_ and _[Kaadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaadu\_(1973\_Kannada\_film) "Kaadu (1973 Kannada film)")_ and most recent film _Kanooru Heggaditi_ (1999), based on a novel by Kannada writer [Kuvempu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuvempu "Kuvempu").

His Hindi movies include _[Nishaant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nishaant "Nishaant")_ (1975), _[Manthan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manthan "Manthan")_ (1976), _[Swami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swami\_(1977\_film) "Swami (1977 film)")_ (1977), and _[Pukar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pukar\_(2000\_film) "Pukar (2000 film)")_ (2000). He has acted in a number of [Nagesh Kukunoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagesh_Kukunoor "Nagesh Kukunoor") films, starting with _[Iqbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iqbal\_(film) "Iqbal (film)")_ (2005), where Karnad's role of the ruthless cricket coach got him critical acclaim. This was followed by _[Dor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dor\_(film) "Dor (film)")_ (2006), _[8 x 10 Tasveer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8\_x\_10\_Tasveer "8 x 10 Tasveer")_ (2009) and _[Aashayein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aashayein "Aashayein")_ (2010). He played a key role in movies _[Ek Tha Tiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ek\_Tha\_Tiger "Ek Tha Tiger")_ (2012) and its sequel _[Tiger Zinda Hai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger\_Zinda\_Hai "Tiger Zinda Hai")_ (2017) produced by [Yash Raj Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yash_Raj_Films "Yash Raj Films").

Karnad has acted in the Kannada gangster movie _[Aa Dinagalu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aa\_Dinagalu "Aa Dinagalu")_.

## Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Controversies")]

At the Tata Literary Festival held in [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai") in 2012, Karnad was invited to speak about "his life in theater" in an hour-long session. During his speech, he lashed out at [V. S. Naipaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul "V. S. Naipaul") for his "antipathy towards Indian Muslims". Naipaul had earlier been conferred the Lifetime achievement award by the festival's organisers. Karnad also criticized the organizers for having honored Naipaul. The audience, which had gathered to hear Karnad speak, had mixed reactions to the speech. Some, like organizer [Anil Dharker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anil_Dharker "Anil Dharker"), tried ineffectually to steer the speech toward less controversial waters. Others were amused by the episode, and some commented on the research and logic that had gone into the speech (unfortunately overshadowed by its 'scandalous' nature).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-ie-24)

Just a few weeks after this, Karnad again created controversy by claiming that [Rabindranath Tagore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore "Rabindranath Tagore"), who wrote India's national anthem, was a great poet but a second-rate playwright.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-dc-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-26)

In November 2015, during celebrations marking the anniversary of 18th-century Muslim ruler [Tipu Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipu_Sultan "Tipu Sultan")'s birth, Karnad stated that [Bangalore International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kempegowda_International_Airport "Kempegowda International Airport") should have been named after Tipu Sultan instead of [Kempe Gowda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kempe_Gowda_I "Kempe Gowda I"). This created a furore among many people. Karnad apologised the following day.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-28)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Personal life")]

While working in Madras for Oxford University Press on his return from England, Karnad met his future wife Saraswathi Ganapathy at a party. They decided to marry but the marriage was only formalised ten years later, when Karnad was 42 years old. Saraswathi was born to a [Parsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsi "Parsi") mother, Nurgesh Mugaseth, and a [Kodava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodava_people "Kodava people") Hindu father, Kodandera Ganapathy.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-ourkarnataka-29) The couple had two children. They lived in [Bengaluru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengaluru "Bengaluru").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5) He was extremely fluent and well-versed in [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada "Kannada"), [Konkani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konkani_language "Konkani language"), [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi"), [Marathi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathi_(language) "Marathi (language)"), and English.

## Activism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Activism")]

He was a proponent of multiculturalism and freedom of expression. He was a critic of [religious fundamentalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_fundamentalism "Religious fundamentalism"). He had publicly condemned the [demolition of Babri Masjid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demolition_of_Babri_Masjid "Demolition of Babri Masjid") in 1992 and later spoke against the attempts to create [controversy about the Idgah Maidan in Hubli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubli_Idgah_Maidan_dispute "Hubli Idgah Maidan dispute").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-hin-5) He had opposed [RSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashtriya_Swayamsevak_Sangh "Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh"), [BJP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BJP "BJP") and other organizations on several occasions. He opposed [Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi "Narendra Modi") for the Prime Minister's post in the [2014 parliament elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Indian_general_election "2014 Indian general election").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-:0-30) He was one of the 200 writers who put out an open letter against hate politics and for “diverse and equal India” during the 2019 general elections. With a tube in his nose, he wore a placard saying "Me Too Urban Naxal"[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-31) at the first death anniversary of slain journalist [Gauri Lankesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauri_Lankesh "Gauri Lankesh").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-:0-30) Karnad claimed that [Tipu Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipu_Sultan "Tipu Sultan") was the greatest king Karnataka had in 500 years, on a religious controversy about the king.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-:0-30) Karnad was a supporter of the Forum for Communal Harmony.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-32)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Girish_Karnad&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Death")]

Karnad died on 10 June 2019 at Bengaluru at the age of 81 due to multiple organ failure following prolonged illness.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-33) "After a discussion with his son, it was made clear to us that his last wish was to not have any floral procession, VVIPs or visits of any dignitaries. Hence, it will be a simple affair."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girish_Karnad#cite_note-34)
